\subsection{TOST Bootstrap Stability}\label{app:tost-bootstrap}

To verify that the equivalence conclusions in \S\ref{app:tost} are not sensitive to sample composition, we assess their stability under bootstrap resampling.
For each of four representative features, we run 1{,}000 bootstrap iterations (base seed\,=\,42): each iteration independently resamples with replacement from the gen-1 and gen-2+ pools, recomputes Cohen's $d$ and the TOST $p$-value (equivalence margin $|d| < 0.20$).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\footnotesize
\caption{Bootstrap stability of TOST equivalence ($B{=}1{,}000$, margin $|d|{<}0.20$). Rejection rate = fraction of bootstrap iterations where TOST rejects non-equivalence at $\alpha{=}0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-bootstrap}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{l c c c}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Rejection rate} & \textbf{Median $d$} & \textbf{$d$ 95\% CI} \\
\midrule
entropy\_max  & 100\% (1000/1000) & 0.062  & [0.037, 0.088] \\
entropy\_min  & 100\% (1000/1000) & $-$0.016 & [$-$0.042, 0.011] \\
tail\_decay   & 100\% (1000/1000) & 0.088  & [0.065, 0.111] \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & 0\% (0/1000)      & 0.458  & [0.435, 0.479] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

All three near-stationary features achieve a 100\% rejection rate across 1{,}000 bootstrap iterations, and their effect-size 95\% CIs fall entirely within the $\pm 0.20$ equivalence margin.
Entropy std, included as an intermediate control, is never rejected (0\%), with its CI $[0.435, 0.479]$ lying entirely outside the margin.
No feature exhibits boundary-crossing: the classification of each feature is unanimous across all bootstrap samples, confirming that the equivalence conclusions are robust to resampling variability.

This appendix validates the causal predictive power of DDR features through three complementary analyses: permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention.

\paragraph{Permutation Importance.}
Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance} reports the mean F1 drop when each feature's values are randomly shuffled across the test set (baseline F1\,=\,0.771).
Drifting features dominate: their average F1 drop (0.187) is $5.5\times$ larger than the near-stationary average (0.034), confirming that location-shift features, not shape features, drive depth classification.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcr}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Group} & \textbf{Mean F1 Drop} & \textbf{Rank} \\
\midrule
hapax\_ratio  & Drifting      & 0.235 & 1 \\
entropy\_mean & Drifting      & 0.170 & 2 \\
ttr           & Drifting      & 0.156 & 3 \\
entropy\_max  & Near-stat.    & 0.070 & 4 \\
entropy\_std  & Intermediate  & 0.057 & 5 \\
entropy\_min  & Near-stat.    & 0.019 & 6 \\
tail\_decay   & Near-stat.    & 0.014 & 7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Permutation importance (8-gen LOGO). Each feature is shuffled independently; the resulting F1 drop quantifies marginal importance. Drifting features average $0.187$ vs.\ near-stationary $0.034$ ($5.5\times$).}
\label{tab:perm-importance}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger Causality.}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} reports Fisher-combined $p$-values from panel Granger causality tests (lag\,=\,1) across 8 generators ($N$\,=\,29{,}095).
Six of seven features exhibit significant Granger causality ($p < 0.001$), meaning past feature values predict future depth beyond what past depth alone explains.
The sole exception is entropy\_min ($p$\,=\,0.375), providing additional evidence for its near-stationary classification: it carries neither large marginal importance (Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance}, rank 7) nor temporal predictive direction.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Combined $p$} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta R^2}$ & \textbf{Significant} \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & $< 0.001$ & 0.031 & Yes \\
hapax\_ratio  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
ttr           & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_mean & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_max  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
tail\_decay   & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_min  & $0.375$   & ---   & No  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Granger causality (Fisher combined across 8 generators, lag\,=\,1, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). $\Delta R^2$ is reported where available.}
\label{tab:granger}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Key Findings.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Drifting dominance.} The $5.5\times$ permutation-importance gap confirms that drifting features (entropy\_mean, ttr, hapax\_ratio) are the primary depth signal carriers, consistent with the DDR partition derived from convergence analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

\item \textbf{Entropy\_min lacks causal direction.} Beyond its small effect size (F1 drop\,=\,0.019), entropy\_min is the only feature without significant Granger causality ($p$\,=\,0.375). This strengthens the near-stationary classification: the feature is neither marginally important nor temporally predictive.

\item \textbf{Entropy\_max asymmetry.} Entropy\_max ranks fourth in permutation importance (F1 drop\,=\,0.070) but produces the largest degradation in the counterfactual intervention ($-$2.0\,pp), indicating that it provides unique signal not redundant with other features; its causal contribution exceeds its marginal importance.

\item \textbf{Mistral heterogeneity.} In per-generator Granger tests, Mistral-7B shows non-significant hapax\_ratio and ttr ($p > 0.4$), though Fisher combination across generators remains significant. This generator-specific attenuation partly explains Mistral's lowest LOGO F1 (0.605) and suggests that DDR fingerprints are weaker in models with heavier repetition penalties.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{9-Generator Scale Evaluation}\label{app:9gen-scale}

This analysis extends the 8-generator LOGO evaluation to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).
All results use class-balanced LOGO; the 8-gen averages here (0.770/0.701) differ slightly from Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} (0.762/0.694), which uses an unfiltered protocol.
Table~\ref{tab:9gen-logo} reports per-generator LOGO performance under this expanded set.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llr cc cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 1.0B & 0.857 & [0.848, 0.866] & 0.785 & --- \\
Qwen3-0.6B      & Qwen    & 0.6B & 0.819 & [0.807, 0.830] & 0.743 & --- \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & Qwen    & 1.7B & 0.811 & [0.800, 0.823] & 0.746 & --- \\
OLMo-2-1B       & OLMo    & 1.5B & 0.773 & [0.762, 0.784] & 0.692 & --- \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3.2B & 0.759 & [0.748, 0.770] & 0.680 & --- \\
Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 8.2B & 0.696 & [0.683, 0.709] & 0.647 & [0.631, 0.664] \\
Gemma-2-2B      & Gemma   & 2.6B & 0.628 & [0.622, 0.634] & 0.440 & [0.432, 0.449] \\
Mistral-7B      & Mistral & 7.0B & 0.605 & [0.593, 0.617] & 0.534 & --- \\
\midrule
\textbf{Average (9-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.751} & & \textbf{0.666} & \\
\textbf{Average (8-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.770} & & \textbf{0.701} & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Overall comparison.}
Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
The per-generator F1 values for the original eight generators shift by at most $[-0.011, +0.002]$, indicating that the inclusion of Gemma data in training does not destabilize existing generalization patterns.

\paragraph{Gemma-2-2B anomaly.}
Gemma-2-2B is the weakest held-out generator: 3-class F1\,=\,0.628, binary F1\,=\,0.440.
Per-class breakdown reveals a striking asymmetry: gen-0 F1\,=\,0.991 and gen-2+ F1\,=\,0.856, but gen-1 F1\,=\,0.036; the classifier almost entirely fails to identify first-generation Gemma continuations.
This is not a data-quality artifact: the Gemma-2-2B partition contains 4{,}957 instances with a balanced depth distribution ($\sim$990 per level).
A plausible explanation is that Gemma-2's first-generation continuations occupy a region of feature space highly similar to human-written text (gen-0), causing systematic misclassification of gen-1 as gen-0 or gen-2+.
This constitutes an architecture-specific generalization limitation rather than a systemic failure of the depth fingerprinting approach.
Several architectural differences may explain this behavior: (a)~Gemma-2's distinct attention mechanism and SentencePiece tokenizer with a larger vocabulary may produce first-generation continuations whose feature-space signature closely resembles human text, causing systematic gen-0/gen-1 confusion; (b)~this anomaly does not affect DDR's validity for the remaining eight generators, where per-generator F1 shifts by at most 0.011 upon Gemma inclusion.

\paragraph{Scale effect.}
A clear parameter-count gradient emerges across the nine generators: three of four sub-1.7B generators achieve F1\,$>$\,0.81 (OLMo-2-1B at 0.773 is the exception), mid-range models (2--3B) cluster at 0.63--0.81, and large models (7B+) fall to 0.60--0.70.
Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters) achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.696 under the 9-gen split, compared to 0.701 in the class-balanced 8-gen evaluation; this small difference reflects the changed training composition rather than a property of the Qwen3-8B generator itself.

59	The partition is demonstrated for this seven-feature set; alternative features (e.g., syntactic complexity, n-gram frequencies) may yield different groupings, though the convergence of five independent effect-size metrics suggests the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.

62	\centering
63	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
64	\caption{Differential depth response (DDR). Per-generator strip widths show cross-generator consistency of the partition.}
65	\label{fig:feature-drift}
66	\end{figure}
67	
68	Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
69	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
70	while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
71	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
72	The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
73	
74	\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
75	Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
76	Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
77	Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
78	Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
79	Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
80	Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
81	The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
82	Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
83	Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) confirms these equivalence conclusions are robust: all three near-stationary features achieve 100\% rejection rate, with effect-size CIs well within the $d{=}0.20$ margin (Appendix~\ref{app:tost-bootstrap}).
84	Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.
85	
86	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}

88	Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).

The partition is demonstrated for this seven-feature set; alternative features (e.g., syntactic complexity, n-gram frequencies) may yield different groupings, though the convergence of five independent effect-size metrics suggests the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response (DDR). Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth reveal a 6$\times$ magnitude gap: drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean; $|\rho| > 0.60$, Cohen's $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) show strong monotonic depth sensitivity, while near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min; $d < 0.10$) remain stable across depths. Entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) occupies a sole intermediate position. This location/shape asymmetry is the basis for depth classification. Per-generator strip widths show cross-generator consistency of the partition.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) confirms these equivalence conclusions are robust: all three near-stationary features achieve 100\% rejection rate, with effect-size CIs well within the $d{=}0.20$ margin (Appendix~\ref{app:tost-bootstrap}).
Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.
TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) show permutation importance differences (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) due to feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}; all three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.
Pythia generators' highest F1 (0.718--0.724) may partly reflect same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model, but the 0.013 cross-reference spread bounds this effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though this does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).
Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).

\label{sec:results-baselines}

Do existing detection methods already capture depth signal?
To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The 7-feature ensemble exceeds all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp; Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}).
Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher binary F1 (0.708 vs.\ 0.705) at 2.4$\times$ inference cost, suggesting depth information is implicitly encoded in distributional divergence measures.
DDR's contribution is not classification performance but decomposing depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components, a distinction absent from both binary detection methods and model collapse analyses (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses confirm that DDR features carry causal predictive power beyond correlation: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, and 6/7 features exhibit significant Granger causality across generation depths, with entropy\_min as the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Two diagnostic scenarios illustrate practical utility: (a)~training-data batch auditing, where batches exceeding a gen-2+ proportion threshold trigger review; (b)~provenance tracing, where known gen-0 seeds enable lineage reconstruction through successive depth predictions.
In generator-unknown deployment, the 9.1\,pp per-generator spread represents estimation uncertainty; the ensemble LOGO F1\,=\,0.694 provides a conservative lower bound, stable across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training (F1 drops to 0.723; worst-case per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs, canonically eroding tail coverage as minority modes vanish across retraining generations; inference-chain drift at fixed parameters operates in a qualitatively different regime where drift is fully reversible and shape features remain near-stationary while only location shifts.
This contrast suggests that fixed-parameter sampling imposes stronger shape constraints than retraining, and it is this shape stability that makes depth detection viable: near-stationary features provide an invariant reference against which location drift becomes detectable, whereas model collapse remediation must restore lost tail coverage.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
